newsitem.title: USA: Calif. governor asks delay in listing coho salmon.
newsitem.headline: Calif. governor asks delay in listing coho salmon.

text.p: California Gov. Pete Wilson urged President Clinton Thursday to delay listing the coho salmon under the Endangered Species Act, saying it could cause a "virtual shutdown" of logging and mining in much of the state.

Under a federal court order, the U.S. National Marine Fisheries Service (NMFS) must decide by Friday whether to list the coho salmon in California and Oregon as endangered or threatened under the Endangered Species Act.
If the coho salmon was listed, steps would be taken to protect its habitat and that could affect the activities of the timber and other industries on lands adjoining streams.
The Sierra Club environmental group says the numbers of wild coho salmon in California have fallen from 500,000 50 years ago to fewer than 5,000 now and is urging the NMFS to list the coho salmon.
The NMFS proposed listing the coho as threatened in July last year but has not yet taken a final decision, seen as highly sensitive in an election year.
In a letter to Clinton, Wilson, a Republican, asked him to order the NMFS to reopen the comment period on its proposal to list the coho salmon and to postpone its decision by six months.

"Failure to extend the comment period is likely to result in both a flawed listing decision by NMFS and unnecessary and severe economic hardship and social disruption to many affected communities in California," Wilson wrote.

"The listing could result in a virtual shutdown of logging, mining, ranching and other agricultural activities over large parts of California. Urban water diversions and wastewater treatment operations could be placed equally at risk," he said. All of these activities would be vulnerable to legal action if the coho salmon was listed, he said.

The California Department of Forestry estimates that in central California about half of the state and private timber land base -- estimated at 10.28 billion board feet of timber worth $4.6 billion -- would be off-limits to harvest as a result of a coho salmon listing, according to Wilson. At least seven mills in the area would be affected, he said.
Wilson said California was taking responsible measures to restore habitat and to protect coho and other salmon stocks.

The Sierra Club said Thursday that, under intense pressure from the Pacific coast timber industry, the NMFS had been delaying action on listing the coho salmon for more than a year. In the meantime, commercial fishers had had to eliminate their coho catch in California and Oregon, laying waste to a $150 million industry, it said.

The Sierra Club said a strong coho salmon listing could provide temporary protection for Headwaters Forest, an ancient redwood grove in northern California that has been the focus of a dispute between environmentalists and a logging company.
